A sharp, patient ear and the discipline to stay accurate over long listening sessions
Reliable availability of about 20 hours/week on a part-time basis

Nice to Have:
Prior experience on AI training-data, model-evaluation, or audio/QA annotation projects
A background in language, editing, voice, or audio production

I’m starting a series: The India Tech Recap

Edition one is about the strangest year I have seen in this industry, where Indian IT lost 21% in a single month and Hyderabad added 43 GCCs in the same six months.

I have been in this business since 1995, first in the US and then here since 2008, and I have never watched the two halves of Indian tech move in opposite directions this sharply. On one side, clients are reopening five year contracts in year two because AI changed the maths mid-deal. On the other side, global companies are landing here faster than anyone can lease them floor space.

Cheap capacity is about to get much cheaper, and it will keep getting cheaper. Capability will not.

If you are running or building an India centre right now, which side are you feeling more? The pricing pressure, or the hiring race?

Last night, Automo passed 500,000 users.  it took Nine weeks.

I should be celebrating. Instead, I keep thinking about how different this feels from the last time.  When we built Desygner, reaching our first million users took 13 months.

We were competing with Canva. They built an extraordinary company. From where I sat, their access to capital gave them an enormous advantage in hiring, distribution and the ability to keep investing.  We felt that gap every day.

I know what it feels like to have the ambition and the product, but watch a better resourced competitor pull ahead.  This time, I believe the economics are changing.

I can now take on work that once needed an entire team. Decades of experience help me decide what to build, what to reject and when the AI is confidently wrong.

Our hardest hiring problem is finding more people like my cofounders: people with judgement, ownership and a deep commitment to customers.

We have lived this change ourselves.
- 98 people became 12.
- Two month release cycles became twice a day.
- We rebuilt how we develop, test, review and ship software.

Human judgement matters more than ever.

Here is my prediction:
The next 12 months will be brutal for software companies whose costs and processes assume building software must remain slow and expensive.
- Some will adapt brilliantly.
- Some will cut prices and squeeze margins.
- Some, I believe, will disappear.

Having thousands of employees is a dangerous advantage if your business needs thousands of employees just to stand still.

Customers will ask:
Why am I paying for ten subscriptions, paying to connect them, then paying again for AI to work across them?

That is the integration tax. Businesses pay it in money, time and mistakes.

We are building Automo to remove it. One connected platform for running a business, with agents able to work across it.

Ciao.dev is how we build it.  My background is in systems for financial markets. That experience taught me to care about what happens after the demo: permissions, testing, reliability and what happens when something breaks.

Generating software is only part of the job. Being able to trust it is the part that matters.
We previously spent about US$155,000 a year on software subscriptions, before counting the work of keeping everything connected.  I have never been so damn happy to rethink that entire stack.

500,000 users is a milestone. Earning their trust and giving them a reason to stay is the job.

For every founder told they cannot compete without raising a fortune, I believe your odds are improving.  The next great software company may have fewer employees than its incumbent has recruiters.

Curious whether Automo could replace parts of your stack?  Check out the link in the comment.

And the discovery usually happens at the worst possible moment: mid-audit, or after an employee complaint has already been filed.

It's not negligence. It's that keeping every policy, contract, and process current with changing regulations, across every state or region a company operates in, is a full-time job in itself — one most HR teams are doing on the side of everything else.

AI compliance tools are starting to take that weight off. Platforms like Trakstar, ComplyAdvantage, and Zoho People now monitor regulatory changes automatically, flag outdated policies before they become liabilities, and keep an audit-ready paper trail on hiring, termination, and disciplinary decisions — the exact documentation that saves a company when a dispute does arise.

It doesn't replace legal judgment. It just means compliance gaps get caught in a quarterly review, not during an actual audit.

Hollywood’s unions are forcing a part of the AI debate into territory that is far less speculative than the question of what artificial intelligence might eventually become.

In June, SAG-AFTRA members ratified their new TV/Theatrical agreement with 91.42% approval. Among its provisions are stronger restrictions on synthetic performers and additional protections around digital replicas.

Producers wishing to use a synthetic in a human role must notify the union and bargain over its use, while the agreement establishes a principle favouring human performance. The WGA’s 2026 agreement moves into another part of the value chain: companies must now notify the Guild when writers’ work is licensed to train a commercial generative-AI system. 

These developments interest me because Hollywood is effectively asking a different AI-risk question. Much of the technology debate concentrates on the capabilities machines may acquire: autonomy, increasingly sophisticated reasoning and, at the extreme, whether future systems could become difficult for humans to control.

Creative workers are confronting the inverse question: as machines acquire more capabilities, what do humans retain control over?

Consider an actor’s face or voice. Historically, accessing the economic value of a performance generally required hiring the performer. Digital replication begins to separate the two. A person can perform once, while a technological representation of elements of that performance may potentially be reused elsewhere.

The economic asset is therefore no longer only labour. It can also become the reproducible digital representation of labour.

That changes the bargaining problem profoundly. Compensation is one issue, but so are consent, duration of use, ownership, reuse and the circumstances under which a synthetic alternative can substitute for another human engagement. SAG-AFTRA itself frames its AI guardrails around consent, compensation and control.
 
Writing introduces a related complication. Once existing creative work can contribute to systems capable of producing new outputs, the boundary between creation and productive input becomes harder to ignore. The WGA’s notification provision is significant precisely because it begins bringing the licensing of that input into the contractual relationship.
 
This is why I would not separate today’s labour disputes from the larger AI-risk conversation. They operate on different timescales, but they concern the same underlying allocation of power: what machines are permitted to do, what humans continue to control, and which institutions define the boundary between the two.

Long before we know whether humanity can retain control over the most advanced AI systems, contracts such as these are already determining something much more immediate:

- How much control humans retain over the economic value of their own identity and creative work.

Remote is a work arrangement. It is not automatically a hiring jurisdiction.

Across years in HR leadership and recruitment, I have seen how one word in a vacancy can create the wrong expectation.

A role is marked “remote,” so candidates understandably assume that location is no longer a barrier. But the employer may still be able to hire in only a limited number of countries.

Consider Epoch AI’s current Recruiter/Senior Recruiter vacancy⁠.

It is fully remote and says the organisation can employ people in many countries. It also explains that contracts and payments are usually localised.

That distinction matters.

The lesson is not that every remote job must be open worldwide. It is that flexibility and eligibility are different promises.

A clear remote vacancy should tell candidates:

Which countries or time zones are eligible?

Will they be employees or contractors?

In what currency will they be paid?

What travel or working-hour overlap is expected?

This information does more than improve candidate experience. It reduces unsuitable applications, protects the employer’s reputation and gives recruiters a more credible process to manage.

Before publishing your next remote vacancy, imagine that the strongest candidate lives in Abuja.

Can they tell from the advert whether you can legally employ and pay them?

If not, the job may be remote, but the opportunity is still unclear.

Global Capability Centres (GCCs) in India are executing a major workforce recalibration, moving away from low-complexity execution and aggressively hiring for specialized engineering and artificial intelligence.

The Core Numbers
 * ~25,000 to 30,000 Cuts: Concentrated in routine, repetitive, and transactional roles—representing roughly 1% of the total 2.6 million GCC workforce in India.
 * ~150,000 New Openings: High-value, specialized tech positions projected to be added in parallel, making GCCs the primary engine of India's technology hiring growth.
 * Net Expansion: Rather than a downsizing wave, the sector is experiencing a net headcount addition of around 120,000 jobs, alongside a sharp rise in average compensation and skill thresholds.

What Is Being Trimmed
The reductions are driven primarily by AI productivity gains, parent-firm operational restructuring, and consolidation among smaller, legacy captive units:
 * Transactional Back-Office Operations: Purchase-to-pay (P2P), basic invoice processing, routine payroll, and entry-level compliance tasks.
 * First-Line Support & Routine IT: Tier-1 IT helpdesk, commodity infrastructure monitoring, and manual QA/testing cycles being taken over by automated pipelines.
 * Commodity Analytics: Basic reporting and manual dashboard maintenance, now largely automated via self-serve business intelligence and generative AI platforms.

Why the Shift Is Accelerating
 * Internalization Over Outsourcing: Multinationals are increasingly cutting third-party IT vendor contracts and bringing core engineering in-house to their captive Indian units.
 * AI Maturity Pressure: As enterprises move from speculative GenAI pilots to full production workloads, GCCs require senior architects who understand compute budgets, low-latency deployment, and data governance.
 * Productivity Arbitrage: Because AI tools allow smaller teams to deliver the same software output, firms are swapping large teams of entry-level coders for leaner teams of high-leverage specialists.

Where the 150K Roles Are Concentrating
​Multinationals are increasingly treating Indian GCCs as global headquarters for core engineering, moving beyond cost arbitrage to business ownership:

Hiring AI agents is no longer science fiction. G42, the UAE's tech giant, is now letting AI agents apply for jobs, complete with a probationary period and performance assessment.

Meanwhile at Think 2026, IBM's CEO drew a line in the sand: "The enterprises pulling ahead are not deploying more AI." They're orchestrating it.

KPMG has scaled trusted enterprise agents globally with Microsoft's Agent 365. SAP is shipping an "Autonomous Enterprise" platform. Workday's agents now act across finance, HR, and policy workflows. Deloitte's State of AI in the Enterprise confirms the gap between intent and execution is widening.

So how should your company plan for AI agents in the workforce?

1. Appoint a human owner for every agent you deploy. Accountability is the new governance.
2. Design for orchestration, not replacement. The leaders aren't swapping headcount; they're rebuilding workflows end to end.
3. Reskill before you reduce. Close the intent-to-execution gap on your terms, not the market's.
4. Cost-watch the compute. Nvidia itself admits AI is still more expensive than people in many roles. Pick workloads where agents genuinely beat labour cost.
5. Keep a human-in-the-loop contract. The billion-dollar companies Gartner surveyed are keeping a human checkpoint for consequential decisions.

The question for boards in 2026 is no longer "Will we use AI agents?" It's "Who is responsible for them, and how do we know they're working?"

That's the conversation we should be having.

#MarginPressure is still a big issue. #US law-firm revenue rose by 12.4% in H1 2026, but expenses grew 9.6%, inventory went up 17.7%, and collections fell 5%.

Recent cyber incidents affecting more than five major law firms exposed sensitive client and personal data. As AI becomes routine, firms need to strengthen #DataSecurity, source checks, access controls and governance.

Our full research on the website can give you a broader view of September’s challenges.

Moreover, entry-level hiring at large U.S. firms fell by 7.5%, which adds pressure as the usual talent pipeline shifts.

The legal-tech market is expected to grow from $31B in 2026 to about $70B by 2033, with roughly 20% of large corporate law firms building customised AI tools. 

Firms are trying to connect contracts, precedents, research, evidence and proprietary knowledge to AI systems, while major platforms move toward joined-up workflows for research, drafting, evidence and matter management. But tying all that knowledge together makes these solutions harder to build.

🚨 Why are so many businesses struggling to hire the right tech talent?

The problem isn't always a lack of candidates.

Often, it's finding the right candidate with the right technical skills, experience and cultural fit — at the right time.
Technology hiring has become increasingly competitive, particularly across AI, Software Engineering, Cloud, Cybersecurity and Data.
For employers, some of the biggest challenges include:

🔹 Skills shortages – specialist technology professionals can be difficult to identify and attract.
🔹 Competition for talent – strong candidates are often considering multiple opportunities.
🔹 Time-to-hire – lengthy recruitment processes can result in businesses losing high-quality candidates.
🔹 Technical assessment – a CV doesn't always demonstrate whether someone has the technical capability required.
🔹 Cultural fit – technical ability is important, but so are communication, commercial awareness and long-term suitability.

So, how can businesses improve tech hiring?
A successful recruitment strategy should go beyond simply advertising a vacancy.
Businesses should:
✅ Clearly define the technical requirements
✅ Target the right talent market
✅ Pre-screen candidates before interviews 
✅ Technically qualify candidates
✅ Assess competency and communication skills
✅ Maintain an efficient interview process
✅ Build talent pipelines before vacancies become urgent

The worst time to realise your business has outgrown its legal setup is just after Sales wins its biggest customer… now Procurement’s involved and they want answers from YOU.

Like the contract, 90-day payment terms, unlimited liability, service levels Ops haven’t seen and the thing Steve from Sales promised when he said: “that shouldn’t be a problem.”

Now it’s Friday's problem and the old way of doing things is getting tougher.

It happens when a growing business starts winning bigger clients.

The outside lawyer can’t just check the odd contract and you can’t know every customer.

So you think about how much you want this revenue, what Ops can actually deliver, the risks that could hurt you, which clauses probably won’t matter… 

Now you need more than someone checking the contract.

I’ve seen companies spend weeks arguing about legal points while the deal leaves without them noticing and businesses sign because they’re scared to lose the client, then six months later realise winning the customer was the easy bit.

That’s the awkward stage of scaling, when your company is too complicated to keep making decisions off the cuff but hiring another full-time senior feels like too much.

Over the next few years, more businesses will find themselves in this position, with AI making it easier and quicker to get the first legal answer.

The valuable bit is knowing what that answer means for you, this customer, this profit margin and this business.

So if you’ve just won the biggest customer in your company’s history, celebrate it.

Then ask Steve exactly what he promised… before next Friday.

When your services partner trains 114,000 people on AI, you have bought a dependency nobody put in the contract at TCS. 

Two other firms did something narrower and sharper in August, seven days apart.

HCL Tech became an OpenAI Advanced Partner on 6 August, running 223,000 employees and $14.8 billion in revenue for the year to June. 

On 13 August IBM announced a dedicated OpenAI practice with thousands of consultants and engineers trained through OpenAI certifications, embedding GPT-5.6, Codex and ChatGPT Work into IBM Consulting Advantage. IBM joins OpenAI's Elite partner tier.

Neither party disclosed financial terms.

I want to be careful here, because we hold partner commitments ourselves and I am in no position to be sanctimonious about anyone else's.

The certification is the part worth watching. Training at that scale on one vendor's stack means a firm has chosen a cost structure, a hiring profile and a renewal negotiation it will be living inside for years. Those commitments are hard to unwind, because the bench is the commitment.

The client inherits that choice without being asked. You buy delivery capability and a model dependency arrives attached to it.

What makes the timing interesting is that model capability is converging while switching costs are being built up deliberately. That puts the lock-in at the delivery layer, which is a quieter place for it than the technology layer.

I do not think any of this is wrong. Depth requires commitment, and clients benefit from people who have gone deep on one stack.

If you are shortlisting a services partner this year, ask which certifications their delivery organization holds and how many people hold them. That number tells you what they can build well. It also tells you what they will find expensive to recommend against.

If you want to go GOD-level with API design,
learn these 7 protocols (save now):


1 REST (Representational State Transfer)
↳ Uses resources & standard HTTP methods via a stateless interface
↳ Use cases: CRUD APIs for web & mobile apps

===

2 GraphQL
↳ Lets clients request exactly the data they need
↳ Use cases: apps with complex and/or changing data requirements

===

3 WebSockets
↳ Keeps a bidirectional connection open between client & server
↳ Use cases: chat, multiplayer games & real-time updates

===

4 gRPC (Google Remote Procedure Call)
↳ Calls remote services via strongly typed contracts
↳ Use cases: fast communication between internal microservices

===

5 Webhooks
↳ Sends event notifications from one system to another
↳ Use cases: real-time AI agents & event-driven workflows

===

6 MQTT (Message Queuing Telemetry Transport)
↳ Sends lightweight messages using publish-subscribe messaging
↳ Use cases: IoT devices & unreliable or low-bandwidth networks

===

7 SSE (Server-Sent Events)
↳ Streams updates from a server to a client over HTTP
↳ Use cases: live feeds, notifications & AI response streaming

Anything else you'd add?

===

👋 PS - Want to make your AI agents real-time?

Polling for updates adds unnecessary latency to agent workflows.

Webhooks let your agents react to events as they happen. But running reliable webhook infrastructure means dealing with failed endpoints, retries, security & monitoring.

Svix handles that infrastructure for you, including automatic retries, signing, observability & idempotency support.

🚀 Recruitment is changing. But great recruitment is still about people.
AI can source candidates.
AI can screen CVs.
AI can help identify skills.
But it can't replace a trusted relationship.
And I think that's becoming more important, not less.
In 2026, recruitment is moving towards skills over titles, quality over quantity and technology-supported hiring. At the same time, human connections are becoming increasingly valuable as applications become easier to generate — and harder to differentiate. 
So, what do I do differently?
🤝 I build relationships before there is a vacancy.
I want to understand professionals before I'm trying to place them — and understand my clients before they urgently need someone.
🎯 I look beyond the CV.
What can you actually do? What motivates you? What environment helps you perform? Where do you want your career to go?
💬 I have real conversations.
AI is a fantastic tool, but recruitment decisions affect careers, teams and businesses. That requires listening, challenging and sometimes giving advice people don't necessarily expect.
📊 I bring market knowledge to both sides.
For candidates: career direction, salary expectations, CV and interview support.
For clients: talent availability, realistic expectations, salary benchmarking, Permanent vs Contract/Freelance options and what I'm hearing directly from the market.
❤️ And I stay involved.
From the first conversation to shortlist, interview, feedback, negotiation and beyond.
Not every candidate I speak to will be right for every client.
Not every opportunity will be right for every professional.
And that's exactly the point.
My job isn't to create the most matches.
It's to create the right ones.
So whether you're a Technology professional evaluating your next chapter, a freelancer considering your next project, or a business thinking about the talent you'll need next:
☕ Let's have a conversation before it becomes urgent.
